page: Google Cloud Platform c4a-standard-72-lssd is an ARM-based general-purpose virtual machine designed for scale-out workloads requiring substantial core density and direct-attached storage. Built on the arm64 architecture, this instance features 72 dedicated vCPUs paired with 288.0 GB of system memory, maintaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per core. The instance operates without discrete GPU acceleration and includes no complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

A key hardware attribute of the c4a-standard-72-lssd is its integrated high-speed storage tier, comprising 6,442 GB of local NVMe SSD capacity across 16 local drives. This configuration provides low-latency, high-throughput scratch space and caching directly attached to the host, eliminating network-attached block storage overhead for temporary data sets. System architects should note that local NVMe SSD storage is ephemeral, requiring external persistence mechanisms for stateful durability.

From an operational and efficiency perspective, the ARM64 compute architecture offers resource-dense processing at lower power profiles compared to legacy x86 implementations. The bundling of extensive local NVMe capacity alongside 72 dedicated ARM cores positions this server well for I/O-intensive workloads, distributed NoSQL databases, transactional data processing, real-time analytics engines, continuous integration build pipelines, and high-concurrency container clusters.

It incorporates 6,442 GB of high-speed local NVMe SSD storage across 16 integrated disks, delivering high-throughput, low-latency disk operations directly at the host level without network storage bottlenecks. The instance features no discrete GPUs and provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses. Benefiting from the energy and density efficiencies of ARM processing combined with massive direct-attached ephemeral storage, the c4a-standard-72-lssd is engineered for high-concurrency environments. It is well matched for I/O-heavy database deployments, high-throughput caching systems, batch data processing, distributed analytics nodes, and microservices platforms requiring dedicated hardware execution.
